analysis.one_liner: Requires federal safety testing of liquefied natural gas rail shipments before any rail transport is authorized.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in a House subcommittee after a 2020 federal rule authorized LNG rail cars without the testing this bill required.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Federal Railroad Administration to physically crash-test rail tank cars carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG), study derailment and collision scenarios, and assess the risks to homes, first responders, and environmentally sensitive areas along rail routes — and it would have barred the Transportation Department from authorizing LNG rail shipments or issuing special permits until that review was done and independently checked by the Government Accountability Office. It never advanced past a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school near rail lines through which LNG trains might run, including rural, suburban, and urban communities; first responders who would need special equipment and training to handle an LNG fire; and local emergency planning officials, who would get advance route notifications. Travelers and residents near busy rail corridors also benefit from required testing before any authorization.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities and first responders along rail lines

how_it_helps.text: Requires physical testing of rail tank cars (including the DOT-113 spec) to confirm they can withstand accidents and prevent or limit an LNG release, at multiple speeds and in derailment, front-end, rear-end, side-impact, grade-crossing, puncture, and incendiary-attack scenarios [S3].

Directs the FRA to study how many homes and structures a discharge would endanger in rural, suburban, and urban areas, the cost to communities of the specialized equipment and training first responders would need, and the risks to environmentally sensitive areas crossed by rail tracks [S3].

Bars the Transportation Secretary from issuing any regulation or special permit authorizing LNG rail transport until the study is finished and the Government Accountability Office has independently verified the agencies complied — a window of up to four years after enactment [S3].
Requires a public report listing all federal research on LNG rail transport since 2010, including authors and publication dates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Natural gas producers and exporters who want to ship LNG by rail, and railroads that would carry the traffic, would face a delay of up to four years before shipments could begin. Taxpayers would fund the federal testing and evaluation program.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes studies and reports rather than immediate safety rules; communities near rail lines get no added protection during the years-long evaluation period beyond the prohibition on new authorizations [S3].

The multi-year testing and GAO review requirement would delay a transportation option that shippers argue could move energy supply, and the bill provides no expedited path even if early testing showed the tank cars were safe [S3].

A study mandate with a hard clock (18 months for the evaluation, 2 years for the report, up to 4 years before authorizations) can consume resources without guaranteeing that any resulting rulemaking addresses the identified risks [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main value is a simple one: no LNG trains on the rails until the tank cars have been physically tested under real-world accident conditions and the risks to homes and first responders are documented. That is a deliberate delay, and the delay is the point — it removes the industry's ability to start shipments before the safety record exists. The cost is that it relies entirely on studies and would not itself impose any operating rules, and communities get nothing extra during the review period. As a study-and-hold bill, it is modest but well designed for its purpose.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its rail subcommittee, never got a markup or floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on September 12, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, where no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Democrats, and never advanced to a committee vote or the House floor [S4][S5].

While the bill sat in subcommittee, the Department of Transportation finalized a rule in 2020 authorizing LNG transport in DOT-113 rail tank cars — the exact action the bill was written to hold off until testing was complete.
The bill received no action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas producers, LNG exporters, and the railroads that would haul the tank cars: LNG-by-rail was authorized by federal rule without the physical testing and risk evaluation this bill would have required first.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gas shippers and railroads, not rail-line communities

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.role: Sponsor; Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring safety testing before LNG rail shipments could be authorized.

for.name: 2 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it never reached a committee or floor vote.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials Subcommittee and never brought it to a markup or floor vote — even though the bill's sponsor chaired the committee.

against.name: Department of Transportation (Trump administration)
against.what_they_did: Finalized a rule in 2020 authorizing LNG rail transport in DOT-113 tank cars, the authorization the bill sought to block pending testing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's three supporters were all House Democrats; no Republicans cosponsored, and it never drew a recorded vote that would show how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Natural gas producers and LNG exporters
industries.note: The bill would have delayed LNG rail shipments for up to four years by requiring crash testing and a GAO review first. Shipments were authorized by federal rule in 2020 without that testing, shifting accident risk onto communities along the tracks while the industry gained a new transport route.

industries.industry: Railroads and rail tank car manufacturers
industries.note: Railroads stood to gain new LNG freight traffic once authorized, which the bill would have delayed; tank car builders would have faced scrutiny of the DOT-113 design's real-world performance. The bill imposed no direct costs on them, only postponement of a new market.
